10.1016/j.joep.2018.12.001: Abstract Shah et al. (2012) examined how different forms of scarcity affect attention and borrowing behavior. Results from a series of lab experiments suggested that (1) various forms of scarcity have similar effects on cognition and behavior, (2) scarcity leads to attentional shifts and greater focus (3) scarcity can lead people to over-borrow, and (4) scarcity can lead to cognitive fatigue. Camerer (2018) recently conducted replications of studies from a set of social science papers, and failed to replicate the result on cognitive fatigue from Shah et al. (2012). In this paper, we present high-powered replications of all studies from Shah et al. (2012). We describe which results appear more robust and which results appear to be less robust. We conclude with some thoughts on the value of self-replications.
10.1073/pnas.2206054120: O’Donnell et al. (“ODAL”) (1) claim to audit the “scarcity literature” through a series of replications. We applaud the paper’s goals, but have found many serious issues, raising questions about its conclusions. Notably, the paper fails as an audit of the scarcity literature. i) It includes studies that are not about resource scarcity (or even about scarcity at all). ii) It fails to implement its own selection criteria. iii) It contains analysis errors. iv) Several replications are untrue to the original studies. These issues in ODAL’s original article affect at least 10 out of 20 studies (see Fig. 1; for detailed discussion, see ref. 2). To be clear, we are not asserting that this is an exhaustive list. Quite the opposite. The shockingly high rate of problems already uncovered suggests that there are likely more errors in the audit that we did not catch (but authors of the original studies might identify). Surprisingly—and unfortunately—ODAL’s Correction continues to ignore nearly all of these concerns. These issues are profoundly problematic, casting doubt on the rigor of the entire audit. They cannot be addressed by rhetoric alone.
10.1038/s41562-018-0405-5: This paper suggested that various forms of resource scarcity would have similar effects, and that a scarcity mindset would lead to attentional shifts that might drive behaviours such as over-borrowing, but found no evidence that scarcity-induced focus leads to cognitive fatigue on subsequent tasks.
